overview: From 1914 to 1960, this enormous mountain-and-desert region was never the single, quiet block suggested by the map. Qing-trained governor Yang Zengxin, rival warlords, Sheng Shicai’s Soviet-backed police state, East Turkestan republics, Chinese Nationalists and the new People’s Republic all claimed or exercised different kinds of power. Uyghur oasis farmers and townspeople, Kazakh and Kyrgyz herders, Hui and Han communities, Mongols, Tajiks, Sibe, Russians and others built lives through households, mosques, markets, pasture routes, schools, workshops and underground karez channels. New printing and education widened public argument; war, purges, monopolies and collectivization repeatedly disrupted it. Doctors and healers worked across epidemics and scarce access, while a governor once showed off a supposedly unique flush toilet. The 1960 endpoint is only an atlas id change: Xinjiang’s peoples, institutions and disputes continued.

periods.title: Yang Zengxin’s guarded provincial regime
periods.summary: Qing-trained governor Yang Zengxin kept Xinjiang formally within the Republic of China while governing with great practical independence. He balanced oasis leaders, clerics, hereditary authorities and a small provincial bureaucracy, restricted political organizing and managed trade across the Soviet frontier.

periods.title: Assassination, succession and sharper extraction
periods.summary: Yang was assassinated in 1928. Jin Shuren succeeded him, faced strained finances and governed more intrusively. Political, religious, commercial and local grievances accumulated across a province whose communities had never experienced the same administration in the same way.

periods.title: Rebellions and the first East Turkestan Republic
periods.summary: The Kumul uprising opened overlapping wars among Uyghur, Hui, Han, Kazakh and other forces. A short-lived East Turkestan Republic was proclaimed at Kashgar in 1933; internal divisions, rival armies and Soviet intervention helped defeat it in 1934.

periods.title: Sheng Shicai, Soviet aid and reform promises
periods.summary: Sheng Shicai consolidated power with Soviet military and financial support. His Six Great Policies promised equality, anti-imperialism, peace and construction; schools, publishing and nationality institutions expanded while the security state also grew.

periods.title: Purges, extraction and a geopolitical turn
periods.summary: Mass arrests and executions devastated officials, intellectuals and alleged opponents. Sheng first deepened Soviet dependence, then turned toward Chiang Kai-shek’s Nationalist government after Germany attacked the Soviet Union, leaving residents to absorb another abrupt change of slogans and alliances.

periods.title: The Ili revolt, Three Districts and uneasy coalition
periods.summary: Revolt in Ili created a Soviet-supported administration across the Three Districts. A 1946 coalition with the Nationalist provincial government did not erase rival authority or mistrust. By 1949 the Chinese Civil War made Xinjiang’s political future newly uncertain.

periods.title: Communist incorporation and competing promises
periods.summary: Nationalist military and provincial leaders changed allegiance in September 1949, and the People’s Liberation Army entered. The new government reorganized administration, land, education and political participation while suppressing resistance and building institutions tied much more closely to Beijing.

periods.title: Autonomous region, bingtuan and collectivization
periods.summary: The Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region replaced the province in 1955. The Production and Construction Corps expanded farms and settlement; cooperatives and then communes reorganized work; schooling and writing systems changed. “Autonomy” existed inside a centralized party-state, not outside it.

sections.title: The map’s one color hides many governments

items.text: The exact atlas id is xinjiang, indexed circa 1914 to 1960. In 1914 it is one Polygon with one ring and 197 coordinate positions, spanning roughly 73.68° to 96.34° east. That technical precision does not make the frontier historically exact: the shape is a locator drawn by a modern map dataset.

The imported outline barely changes while authority changes dramatically. The 1920 and 1930 coordinate arrays match exactly; later snapshots have the same one-part, 197-position structure with only tiny transform differences. A stable colored patch can therefore conceal assassination, civil war, rival administrations, revolution and a new constitutional label.

In the 1900 snapshot, Ürümqi, Kashgar, Hotan, Turpan, Yining, Altay, Hami and Aksu all fall inside qing-dynasty. By 1914 the same audited places fall inside xinjiang. The Qing had fallen in 1911, so neither database seam is a magic midnight when a whole society changed identity.

At the 1960 seam, the xinjiang feature disappears and those eight places move to the broad china id. Xinjiang itself did not vanish, and its autonomous-region government had already been created in 1955. The endpoint belongs to this atlas’s filing system, a reminder that databases can have endings that people and places do not.

“Xinjiang,” “Chinese Turkestan,” “East Turkestan,” oasis names and national names carried different political meanings. People could identify by town, religion, language, kin group, livelihood or a newer national category. The card keeps the atlas label for navigation, then refuses to squeeze Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Hui, Han, Mongols, Kyrgyz, Tajiks, Sibe and others into one civilization-shaped box.

sections.title: Governors, rebellions and neighbors with very long arms

items.text: Yang Zengxin ruled through a small provincial administration after 1911, using Qing precedents and bargains with local authorities while keeping revolutionary organizations under tight control. Beijing claimed the province, but the overland journey was enormous and central power weak. “Governor” was the official title; “careful frontier survivor” better describes the daily job.

Modern Uyghur nationhood grew through travel, printing, schools and debate rather than waking fully formed on one date. Reformers and merchants crossed the Russian frontier, encountered Jadid schooling and argued over community names. Oasis identities and being Muslim remained important even as “Uyghur” gained wider political use in the 1920s and 1930s.

The 1933 republic centered on Kashgar was a serious bid for independent government and also a fragile coalition. Leaders disagreed over religion, nationalism, outside allies and even the state’s name. Rival Hui forces, Sheng Shicai’s armies and Soviet intervention defeated it in 1934. A short lifespan does not make its participants’ ambitions imaginary.

Sheng Shicai advertised equality and construction while building police power. Soviet loans, advisers and troops helped him prevail; nationality institutions and schools expanded, but purges later imprisoned or killed officials, intellectuals and suspected rivals. A new textbook and a midnight arrest could both belong to the same modernization campaign.

Soviet, British, Chinese Nationalist and later American officials all watched Xinjiang, but their archives are not a security camera pointed at objective truth. The 1944 U.S. consul separated direct observation from Chinese allegations and judged revolt more plausibly rooted in misrule than wholly manufactured abroad. That caution is itself valuable evidence.

sections.title: Ili revolt, Communist takeover and building a new frontier

items.text: The November 1944 uprising in Ining involved Kazakh, Uyghur, Tatar, Russian and other participants and created a government across Ili, Tarbagatai and Altay, the Three Districts. Soviet arms and advice mattered, but local anger at taxation, monopoly buying and political exclusion mattered too. Calling it only “Soviet-made” erases the residents who fought.

A 1946 agreement formed a coalition provincial government, yet the Three Districts kept separate armed strength and competing goals. A 1947 U.S. report mixed observation, Chinese accusations and inference about Soviet aid. Historians can use it, but should keep the author’s uncertainty labels attached instead of quietly peeling them off.

By June 1949, Nationalist officials in Tihwa were repairing southern roads and discussing withdrawal while relations with Ili leaders remained strained. In September, provincial civilian and military authorities changed allegiance; the PLA entered afterward. Mao’s telegram promised unity and order, language that records the new state’s goals rather than proving a painless transition.

The Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region was inaugurated in 1955, with Uyghur, Kazakh, Mongol, Hui, Kyrgyz, Tajik and Sibe autonomous subdivisions. This created offices and named representation, but sovereignty and final policy remained with the centralized party-state. “Autonomous” on a sign did not mean that every village chose its own laws.

The Production and Construction Corps combined farming, industry, settlement and security. Thousands of demobilized soldiers joined it, and young women were recruited from eastern provinces; some expected army roles but were assigned to construction units and pressured toward frontier family-making. Development plans arrived inside real bodies, marriages and disappointments.

sections.title: Oasis farms, moving herds and a working day

items.text: Most settlement clustered where mountains and rivers made oases possible. Families grew wheat, maize, cotton, fruit and other crops under intensely local water conditions; pastoralists moved sheep, horses, cattle and camels through northern and mountain grasslands. Desert and peaks made a provincial line look much more connected than travel actually felt.

Early twentieth-century markets tied Ili, Aksu, Kashgar and Ghulja to routes beyond the Soviet frontier. Regional fairs offered tea, furs, Indian scarves, Kashgar rugs and even Singer sewing machines. The old Silk Road had acquired customs papers and brand-name hardware; a camel caravan and a sewing-machine salesman could share the same economy.

In the 1940s the provincial purchase network pressed herders to sell wool, pelts and livestock through official channels as Soviet trade contracted. Sheep became especially valuable to government revenue. For a pastoral household, a geopolitical pivot could arrive as a lower buying price, a requisition or an official counting animals beside the corral.

Early PRC policy did not collectivize every livelihood at the same speed. In Altay, pastoral-agricultural cooperatives and public-private pastures expanded between 1952 and 1959, while mobile herding partly continued. New administrative units cut across older clan territories, changing who organized labor, pasture access and mutual help.

Cooperation grew from small household teams into larger collectives, and in 1958 communes reorganized work and distribution. Adults earned work points rather than simply keeping each household’s harvest; herders and oasis farmers experienced this differently. A reform chart may show neat arrows while a family asks the practical question: who gets tonight’s flour?

sections.title: Families, courts, faith and neighborhood life

items.text: There was no “Xinjiang family” template. An oasis farming household, a Kazakh herding camp, a Hui merchant family, a Han official household and a Sibe village could organize work, residence and inheritance differently. War, migration, class and whether a parent was absent with a caravan or army changed family life again.

Republican-era Uyghur divorce cases from Kashgar and Khotan show that Islamic courts handled marriage conflict, maintenance, custody and inheritance, with village elders and fathers-in-law participating. Women appear as legal actors, not merely relatives mentioned in men’s files. The records reveal disputes especially well, so they should not be mistaken for an average peaceful household.

A Kashgar waqf document records a pious endowment: property or income set aside for a religious or charitable purpose. Such papers help reconstruct institutions that supported worship, learning or assistance, but the surviving scroll is incomplete. History sometimes reaches the archive with its first page already missing, which is very rude of history.

In the early PRC, official stories celebrated educated, working and performing Uyghur women as model citizens. Those images opened some public roles while also telling women how a “modern” life should look. Schooling, wage work and political campaigns affected household authority, but a poster’s smiling tractor driver is not a transcript of every woman’s day.

Meshrep offers continuity evidence for social life: gatherings can combine music, dance, stories, food, games, moral teaching and mediation. UNESCO’s description is modern, so it cannot prove that every 1920s town held the same event in the same way. It does show why “entertainment,” “classroom” and “community meeting” need not be separate boxes.

sections.title: Pilaf, bazaar bargaining, clothing, music and play

items.text: Gunnar Jarring remembered Kashgar’s 1929 to 30 food bazaar as open kitchens and simple eating places selling grilled meat, rice, pilaf and pastries. He was a foreign visitor writing later, so this is one city snapshot, not everybody’s diet. Still, it safely answers a child’s urgent historical question: yes, the street food smelled excellent.

The same memoir noticed poor people and beggars moving among the food stalls and connected almsgiving with Muslim practice. A tempting menu therefore also reveals inequality: some bought a meal, some cooked at home, and some waited for charity. “What did people eat?” cannot be separated from “What could this person afford today?”

Crafts occupied different bazaar lanes. Jarring described carpets, embroidered cloth, loose coats, turbans and women’s veiling in Kashgar, while rugs arrived from Khotan, Yarkand, Kashgar and Kyrgyz mountain makers. Clothing expressed religion, locality, gender, work and wealth; no single costume can stand in for a region larger than many countries.

Music and dancing were not merely stage shows. In meshrep, performers and participants could exchange songs, dance, jokes, games and stories while hosts mediated behavior. The tradition’s exact twentieth-century forms varied by oasis and occasion. Imagine a party, talent show, debate club and very opinionated neighborhood court sharing one room.

Children’s recreation rarely survives as a government statistic. Printed “Bulbul’s Story,” school verses and primers show that young readers encountered songs and narrative as well as alphabets; families also passed on games and oral stories. The catalog preserves books better than playground noise, so the card states the imbalance instead of inventing a universal toy.

sections.title: Schools, printing and words that changed alphabets

items.text: Jadid reformers promoted “new-method” schools with quicker literacy teaching and subjects beyond memorized religious texts. Merchants, teachers and travelers connected Kashgar and other oases with Muslim educational experiments across Russia and the Ottoman world. Traditional maktabs and madrasas did not simply vanish; old and new lessons sometimes competed under one roof.

The Swedish Mission press opened in Kashgar in 1912 and was the only modern-equipment press in southern Xinjiang, according to its collection history. Missionaries printed religious works, but also primers, geography, spelling, natural science, silk cultivation and Central Asian history. The source is a mission catalog, so its shelf is not the whole reading world.

A 1936 investigator described children and adults sharing a battered textbook while a secular teacher and local mullah disputed the curriculum. That scene shows both hunger for learning and the thin material base of many schools. One book could be library, lesson plan and peace treaty, until the teachers disagreed about page one.

Authentic Eastern Turki writing sample: “استقلال” ,  transliterated Istïqlāl, meaning “Independence.” It was the title of a 1933 Kashgar periodical printed in an Arabic-derived script. The digitized catalog confirms language, place, publisher and date; this single political word does not represent every local language, handwriting style or opinion.

After 1949, formal education expanded but access, language and curriculum remained unequal. Uyghur writing shifted from an Arabic-derived script toward Cyrillic in the later 1950s, with a Latin-based reform arriving around the atlas endpoint. Adults could become “bad spellers” without forgetting a word, officials had changed the alphabet underneath them.

sections.title: Doctors, remedies, epidemics and care close to home

items.text: Eastern Turki medical manuscripts collected around 1929 to 30 preserve recipes, diagnostic ideas and humoral learning from local textual practice. They sit beside family remedies, religious care and other knowledge that was often transmitted without entering a hospital ledger. A surviving prescription proves a tradition existed; it does not prove how often every household used it.

Swedish missionaries operated hospitals and trained or employed medical staff in Kashgar and Yarkand; one doctor also became known for dentistry. These facilities treated patients and introduced techniques, while conversion remained part of the mission’s purpose. Medical help and missionary ambition can occupy the same building, sometimes in adjoining rooms.

Soviet doctors worked against plague, smallpox and other epidemics and reported on living conditions across multiple communities. Their care could save lives, but Soviet medicine was also foreign policy, and reports often judged patients through “sanitary culture” stereotypes. A thermometer may be objective; the paragraph a doctor writes afterward may not be.

A 1952 state magazine announced free-treatment teams, hygiene instruction, and maternity and child-care work in minority regions including Xinjiang. That records what the new government wanted readers to see. It does not count how many villages a team reached, whether medicine remained stocked, or how patients evaluated the visit.

Care depended on place and money. A city resident might reach a mission, Soviet or government clinic; an oasis family might consult a local healer; a moving herding household could be days from any staffed facility. The sources illuminate institutions and written remedies better than ordinary bedside decisions, so the card leaves room for what the archive missed.

sections.title: Karez water, the famous toilet and an ending that was not an end

items.text: Turpan’s karez systems carried groundwater through gently sloping underground channels, reducing evaporation before water reached fields and homes. Shafts allowed digging and repair. This was not a gadget “discovered” by one famous inventor; generations of specialists had to read soil, slope and water, then keep crawling back underground when a tunnel misbehaved.

Yang Zengxin proposed government-funded repair when provincial finances were weak. The source counts 1,084 working Turpan karez in 1949 and 1,237 in 1957. Those numbers show expansion and maintenance, not equally safe household drinking water everywhere. An irrigation channel can sustain an oasis without becoming a chlorinated kitchen tap.

Toilet tidbit, with a giant warning label: during Henry Wallace’s 1944 visit, TIME reported Governor Sheng proudly demonstrated what publicity called the only flush toilet in all Xinjiang. Treat that as a comic elite boast, not a plumbing census. Most toilets were plainly not flush systems, but the available sources do not justify one universal household design.

The period’s achievements were collective and complicated: farmers and diggers kept oasis water moving; printers made science and schoolbooks in Eastern Turki; teachers widened literacy; musicians sustained social knowledge; clinicians combined local and imported medicine. Governments claimed these successes, but skilled hands in households, workshops, schools and canals did the daily work.

The map stops the xinjiang id at 1960, five years after the autonomous region began. Its replacement by china is a cartographic handoff, not a conquest in 1960 or the end of Uyghur, Kazakh, Hui, Han, Mongol, Kyrgyz, Tajik, Sibe and other communities. Their languages, families, arguments and expertise continued beyond the button’s date.

ending.text: The 1960 endpoint is an atlas id change, not the disappearance of Xinjiang or its peoples. The Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region had existed since 1955 and continued inside the People’s Republic of China after the map began using the broader china id. State institutions, settlement and collectivization transformed daily life, while families, languages, faiths, music, water knowledge and memories continued, sometimes adapting, sometimes resisting and never obeying a tidy database seam.
